independence_rule: Facts were established from the local Book VII chapter text before comparison with production JSON or the Book VII production manifest. Canonical IDs are normalization labels only; reader-facing identity knowledge, reported events, intended actions, mistaken beliefs, rumors and actual outcomes remain distinct.

chapters.title: The Runaway Ox
historical_context: Sekishusai's death is deliberately kept secret until Munenori returns for the funeral
Todo Takatora's recent consolidation of Iga and the disputed Tsukigase boundary
future identity: Ushinosuke intends to become Araki Mataemon

facts.description: Sekishūsai died late the previous year; the Yagyū household is keeping the death secret until Munenori can return for the funeral service.
Inshun warns Sukekurō that men around Tsukigase may be Tōdō retainers pushing the Koyagyū boundary, prompting an investigation.
Ushinosuke reports that the men at Tsukigase are said to be expelled rōnin building cabins rather than Tōdō samurai, weakening the boundary-invasion rumor.
Otsū leaves Koyagyū with Ushinosuke to see the plum blossoms at Tsukigase without first announcing the excursion.
Ushinosuke says he wants to enter samurai service and eventually take the name Araki Mataemon.
Three rōnin recognize Otsū from Kyoto/Yoshioka circles, try to seize her and attack Ushinosuke when he refuses to abandon her.
Ushinosuke fights the rōnin, wounds one, and accidentally cuts the ox, which bolts with Otsū clinging to it.
The man traveling as Inshun's attendant stops the runaway ox on the Kasagi highroad and saves Otsū.
Sukekurō recognizes that the attendant calling himself Torazō is Hamada Toranosuke; Toranosuke asks that his identity remain secret while he performs menial discipline at Hōzōin.

chapters.title: Hemp Seed
historical_context: Takuan's delayed letter reports Musashi's expected shogunal appointment, but a later letter cancels that premise
Hozoin public tournament and seating contest

facts.description: A delayed letter from Takuan tells Otsū that Musashi is expected to become instructor to the shōgun and asks her to come to Edo to help establish his household.
Otsū immediately decides to leave Koyagyū for Edo despite Hyōgo's attempts to persuade her to wait and travel with protection.
Hyōgo tests Ushinosuke in the Yagyū dōjō; the boy shows unusual agility, courage and willingness to accept death under what he believes is a real samurai punishment.
Ushinosuke explains that he developed his jumping ability by daily practice over rapidly growing hemp plants after observing mountain fighters.
A new letter from Takuan reports that Musashi's appointment has been canceled, making the news on which Otsū departed obsolete.
At the Hōzōin tournament Nankōbō defeats Daun and then avoids a dangerous outsider after recognizing the risk.
A dispute over a reed mat leads Iori and Ushinosuke to a private bout near the pagoda; Ushinosuke wins.
Gonnosuke and Sukekurō nearly clash over the boys but deliberately de-escalate after learning the fight was mutually agreed.
Gonnosuke and Iori learn that Otsū left Koyagyū roughly three weeks earlier and that Musashi is no longer known to be in Edo.

chapters.title: Sweepers and Salesmen
historical_context: Kongōji history and Southern/Northern Courts
Hideyoshi's patronage of temple sake
anti-Tokugawa ronin network operating under merchant/priest disguises
physical_locations: Amano River valley and temple bridge
Amami plateau/pass road and gully bridge

facts.description: Gonnosuke travels to Kongōji to arrange a memorial tablet and service for his mother, using Oan and Tōroku as local contacts.
During the memorial service Gonnosuke reaffirms that Musashi has accepted him as a teacher and that he intends eventually to establish his own school.
Looking at the Dainichi image, Iori identifies its face with the woman he met near the Yagyū residence and now believes that woman is his lost sister.
Gonnosuke and Iori meet Kōetsu and Myōshū at Kongōji and exchange news and memories of Musashi.
Kōetsu explains the temple's imperial and civil-war history, prompting Gonnosuke to reflect on the political meaning of the Way of the Samurai.
The white-robed mountain priest who has been following Gonnosuke attacks him with a staff near the temple bridge.
The anti-Tokugawa network mistakes Gonnosuke and Iori for agents sent by Hōjō and labels Gonnosuke a Tokugawa spy.
Sugizō, Gensuke and disguised cord sellers lure Gonnosuke onto a compromised bridge, trap him with hidden ropes and take him alive toward Mount Kudo; Iori escapes into the gully.

chapters.title: A Pear Blossom
historical_context: Sanada Yukimura's former identity and Toyotomi loyalty
Tokugawa-Osaka tension
Hosokawa Yūsai memorial materials at Seiganji

facts.description: Leaving Mount Kōya, Sado reflects on impermanence, Zen and the duty of a samurai to remain engaged with the living world.
Daisuke identifies his father Gessō as the former Sanada Yukimura and invites Sado to the Mount Kudo residence.
Sado accepts Yukimura's hospitality despite knowing a secret meeting between a Hosokawa senior retainer and a major Toyotomi loyalist could be politically dangerous.
Sado and Yukimura discuss Musashi as a rare rōnin whose ideals may matter more than stipend or position.
Yukimura insists he cannot simply transfer loyalty after Hideyoshi's death even while denying exaggerated rumors about his resources and conspiratorial power.
At Kamuro, Benzō openly reports that he captured an Edo spy, inadvertently exposing the clandestine operation in front of Sado.
The supposed priest Rinshōbō is explicitly identified as Toriumi Benzō, one of Yukimura's leading retainers.

chapters.title: The Port
historical_context: Sakai merchant culture and shipping network
Kobayashi service to the Hosokawa house

facts.description: After the ambush separates him from Gonnosuke, wounded Iori reaches the Kishiwada area and is taken in by Osei and Otsuru.
Iori travels by ship from Kishiwada to Sakai and enters the Kobayashi merchant household.
Iori resents merchant-house discipline, refuses to surrender his father's sword and repeatedly rebels against Sahei's attempts to make him a shop boy.
While tied and publicly punished outside the shop, Iori sees Otsū pass very close by but is gagged and unable to call to her.
Namban'ya objects to Iori's public humiliation and forces Sahei to untie him; afterward Iori is allowed to attend a temple school and retain his sword.
Iori recognizes Kojirō among Hosokawa travelers waiting to depart Sakai and deliberately throws hot tea at him, reopening their hostility.
Kojirō suggests boiling water as punishment, but Sado's arrival changes the power balance before the punishment is inflicted.
Sado decides Iori should be raised as a samurai rather than as a merchant's assistant; Osei consents and Iori happily joins Sado for Kokura.

chapters.title: The Writing Teacher
historical_context: Musashi lives under the local name Muka while teaching children
Honda/Yoshioka-linked vendetta
Tōgun Style lineage

facts.description: Musashi lives in Okazaki under the name Muka, teaching reading and writing while practicing calligraphy and sword discipline.
Musashi regularly meets Matahachi, who is seeking Zen discipline at Hachijōji while waiting for Gudō.
Matahachi admits his past wrongs, renounces his claim on Otsū and asks Musashi to marry her and give her the happiness he failed to provide.
Musashi admits that he has reached a profound inner impasse and has been searching for Gudō because ordinary sword progress no longer resolves it.
Yoshioka-connected Honda samurai fire on Musashi at Yahagi Bridge; he kills two attackers and a third escapes.
Watari Shima apologizes on behalf of the Honda house after investigating the unauthorized vendetta and asks Musashi to let the matter end.
Using two muskets as demonstration weights, Musashi explicitly formulates that two swords are one sword because both arms belong to one body and ultimate reasoning is nondual.
Gudō finally returns; Musashi begs for direct instruction, but Gudō says he has 'not one thing' to give and refuses conventional teaching.
Musashi decides the encounter is too important to lose and follows Gudō and Matahachi west on the Tōkaidō toward Kyoto.

chapters.title: The Circle
historical_context: Daitokuji/Daitō Kokushi teaching against clinging to leaves and branches
Gudō's self-mocking Zen verse

facts.description: Musashi follows Gudō for weeks through Mino and Ōmi, sleeping apart and allowing his appearance to deteriorate as part of his desperate search for one decisive teaching.
Musashi recognizes that his obsessive pursuit of a single answer may itself be another attachment to 'leaves and branches.'
At the Mount Hiei pass Gudō refuses explanation and instead draws a circle around the kneeling Musashi before walking away.
Musashi initially hates Gudō's apparent cruelty, then studies the circle and realizes that self and universe, one sword and two swords, are not separate.
The circle dissolves Musashi's mental wall: he understands his previous impasse as a shadow of the confused mind rather than an external barrier.
Musashi starts after Gudō to apologize and then stops, recognizing even that impulse as another branch rather than the root of the insight.

chapters.title: Shikama Blue
historical_context: Mambei's story about Ogin is a deliberate lure
Jōtarō now uses the name Aoki Jōtarō and serves after his father's reinstatement

facts.description: After failing to find Musashi in Edo, Otsū has reached Shikama and supports herself with a dyer's household while continuing to search for him.
Mambei falsely claims Ogin is nearby with secret news from Musashi and persuades Otsū to travel with him to Mikazuki.
At the Mikazuki shrine Mambei delivers Otsū into Osugi's ambush; Hon'iden men bind her and begin taking her toward Shimonoshō.
Jōtarō reappears as an older young samurai, confronts Osugi over years of persecution and reveals that his father Aoki Tanzaemon has been reinstated.
Jōtarō explicitly refuses to kill Osugi because doing so would dishonor his restored father, choosing punishment and rescue over revenge killing.
Jōtarō confines Osugi in a cave, uses a written message as leverage, pursues the abductors and demands Otsū's release.
Jōtarō fights the Hon'iden men; Otsū frees herself and assists with stones, while Jōtarō kills or seriously wounds multiple attackers and rescues her.
Otsū stops Jōtarō from pursuing and killing a wounded fleeing opponent, reasserting mercy immediately after her rescue.
At the Mikazuki inn Jōtarō tells Otsū that Musashi is expected to pass toward Kokura for a challenge against Kojirō and urges her to anticipate rather than merely trail his movements.

chapters.title: The Mercy of Kannon
historical_context: Kannon devotional tradition
Tenjinzan Castle conflict and the memorial inscription of Mori Kinsaku's mother

facts.description: Despite Osugi's persecution, Otsū leaves the inn in a violent storm and returns alone to the shrine because she fears the old woman may die in the cave.
Otsū locates Osugi and works to remove the rocks while reassuring her through the storm.
Even after learning Otsū came to save her, Osugi interprets the act as manipulation and again demands that Otsū return to the Hon'iden family as Matahachi's wife.
After escaping the cave, Osugi attacks and beats Otsū until the younger woman becomes unconscious and appears dead.
Alone with Otsū's seemingly dead body and confronted by a mother's memorial inscription, Osugi realizes that devotion to her own son turned her into a monster toward another woman's child.
Osugi explicitly recognizes that she misread Otsū's goodness as evil, begs forgiveness and rejects her former self-justifying interpretation of events.
Rather than remain in despair, Osugi decides Otsū may still be alive and calls for help so she can be treated.
The Hon'iden search party finds Osugi; she immediately orders them to focus on saving the unconscious Otsū rather than on her own safety.

chapters.title: The Tides of Life
historical_context: Date explicitly early fourth month 1612
public construction of Musashi-vs-Kojirō rivalry

facts.description: Musashi departs Sakai by regular ship toward Shimonoseki/Kokura for the long-negotiated bout with Kojirō.
Musashi reflects that public fame and supporters have turned the confrontation into a social spectacle he neither sought nor fully controls.
He checks his resentment by recognizing that his survival, clothing and food all depend on other people's labor and goodwill.
Gonnosuke reaches Sakai too late for Musashi's ship and explains that Yukimura recognized the false spy accusation, released him and helped search for Iori.
Kōetsu tells Gonnosuke that Iori is alive and living with Sado in Kokura.
In Osaka Matahachi unexpectedly sees Akemi impoverished and selling seafood with a baby on her back.
Matahachi calculates that the child may have been conceived while they lived together in Edo and chooses to treat himself as the father, although biological paternity is not established.
Matahachi gives up the attempt to become a formal priest, returns his robe and prayer beads and decides to work, support Akemi and raise the child in ordinary life.
Matahachi explicitly understands Gudō's teaching that religious discipline can continue amid the lies, conflict and impurity of ordinary society.

chapters.title: The Evening Boat
historical_context: Osugi's false Ogin story is explicitly admitted
Musashi's ship is expected to make a regular Shikama stop but instead does not disembark

facts.description: Osugi's repentance proves durable: she nurses Otsū, treats others more kindly and becomes respected rather than feared.
Osugi publicly nullifies Matahachi's old betrothal to Otsū and destroys the written marriage promise.
Osugi now openly says Musashi is the proper husband for Otsū and plans to apologize to him and entrust Otsū to him.
Otsū, Osugi and Jōtarō wait at Shikama hoping to meet Musashi during his ship's scheduled stop.
Musashi speaks to a Himeji messenger from the ship but refuses to disembark because he and the captain want to reach Kokura promptly; Otsū misses him again.
After hearing the ship has already continued west, Otsū converts despair into determination and decides to go to Kokura and witness the bout herself, even while ill.

chapters.title: A Falcon and a Woman
historical_context: Ganryu Style's rapid spread through Kyushu
public debate over Kojirō and Musashi
Funashima selected as controlled duel site

facts.description: Kojirō has become chief sword instructor in practice while treating the older Ujiie Magoshirō with outward deference and sharing instruction duties.
Praise of Musashi provokes Kojirō into repeated public attacks on Musashi's character and Ichijōji conduct, helping turn rivalry into expected confrontation.
At Tadatoshi's order Kojirō has formally challenged Musashi, and the fief council is now finalizing the controlled bout.
Kakubei tells Kojirō the bout will occur on Funashima because an island can restrict crowds and intervention.
Kojirō refuses Kakubei's suggestion to inspect Funashima beforehand, arguing that fixed precautions reduce freedom and can themselves be anticipated.
Kakubei confronts Kojirō about Omitsu; Kojirō admits their relationship and Kakubei proposes marriage after the bout.
Kakubei treats marriage to Omitsu as the next step after victory, while Kojirō remains privately aware she could be left behind if he dies.
Kojirō uses solitary falconing with Amayumi to steady himself and draws martial confidence from the bird's predatory focus.
Despite outward confidence, Kojirō increasingly thinks about Omitsu, his dead mother and the possibility of his own death.

chapters.title: Before the Thirteenth Day
historical_context: Official fourth-month 1612 duel notice fixes day, time and Funashima restrictions
Kojirō's aunt raised him after his mother's death

facts.description: The Hosokawa government posts the formal order for the thirteenth-day, eight-o'clock Funashima bout and prohibits supporters and civilian boats from approaching.
Matahachi and Akemi reach Kokura as a poor but visibly stable household, traveling with the baby and making a living modestly.
Gempachi recognizes Matahachi from the period when he falsely called himself Sasaki Kojirō; Matahachi now looks back on that impersonation with shame rather than pride.
Gempachi comes from Kōzuke to support Kojirō and recounts the lineage connecting Kojirō to Kanemaki Jisai and the Chūjō tradition.
Kojirō has written two last testaments, one for Kakubei and one for Omitsu, and chooses Tatsunosuke as his allowed attendant.
Kojirō receives the aunt who raised him; she frames the bout as decisive for the honor of the Sasaki family and brings a protective underrobe made by supporters.
Surrounded by admirers and gifts, Kojirō becomes psychologically burdened by the repeated inner command that he must win.
Late news reaches Kojirō's crowded house that Musashi has arrived in the Moji/Kokura area.

chapters.title: At Daybreak
functional_actors: Kojirō supporter spying on the gathering
historical_context: Annual former-Shimmen-retainer horseshoe ceremony remembers Sekigahara defeat, Hosokawa patronage and survival through menial work

facts.description: Musashi crosses from Shimonoseki to Moji to confirm acceptance of the time and place of the bout, but declines to wait for Sado.
Musashi unexpectedly reunites with Iori, gives him serious guidance about education, restraint, life and honorable service, and accepts that the conversation may be their final farewell.
Former Shimmen retainers who knew Munisai find Musashi and invite him to their annual private memorial gathering.
Musashi refuses a public evening at Sado's house because rumors already cast the duel as a factional contest between Sado and Kakubei; he does not want to compromise either man.
The former Shimmen men repeat the horseshoe-making ritual that commemorates poverty after Sekigahara, gratitude to Hosokawa Sansai and loyalty to the vanished Shimmen house.
After the gathering Musashi deliberately keeps out of public view, causing Sado and others to fear he has fled.
When found at Tarōzaemon's house, Musashi refuses Sado's official boat because accepting it could make Sado appear to oppose Tadatoshi; he will use a private Kobayashi boat instead.
Sado allows Iori to accompany him to Funashima on the condition that the boy remain composed even if they must retrieve Musashi's corpse.
Matahachi and Akemi learn from Nuinosuke that Musashi has not fled and take position on a hill from which they hope to watch the distant bout.

chapters.title: The Marriage
historical_context: Kojirō discards devotional charms to remove psychological obligations
Musashi paints immediately before departure as an expression of selfless concentration

facts.description: Kojirō leaves Kokura for Funashima in Tadatoshi's specially prepared boat with Tatsunosuke and the falcon Amayumi.
Halfway out Kojirō releases Amayumi toward the castle and discards protective charms, including his aunt's underrobe, so that only his 'naked self' remains for the fight.
While others panic over the time, Musashi calmly finishes two paintings and treats the act as discipline in letting a selfless heart act without ego.
Musashi chooses Tarōzaemon's private boat and the secluded Heike Pine departure point to avoid spectacle and factional entanglement.
Osugi apologizes for years of hatred; Musashi forgives her and asks forgiveness for the trouble he caused her, freeing both from the old vendetta.
Musashi and Otsū meet face to face at the Heike Pine after years of separation; Musashi openly admits that apparent coldness did not mean lack of love.
Otsū asks Musashi to say that she is his wife for life; he silently assents and immediately frames the departure in terms of the duty of a samurai's wife and her husband's possible final departure.
After Musashi boards Sasuke's boat, Otsū composes herself, kneels on the beach and sends him away without regrets; Osugi, Gonnosuke and Jōtarō bow with her.

chapters.title: The Soul of the Deep
historical_context: Final duel occurs around ten o'clock despite the official eight-o'clock appointment
narrator explicitly leaves later revenge-attempt claims unresolved
physical_locations: boat from Shimonoseki through Kanmon strait

facts.description: Musashi travels toward Funashima with the rising/turning tide and is satisfied that the late arrival will place him there around ten.
During the crossing Musashi carves a broken oar into the wooden sword he will use against Kojirō.
Before landing Musashi leaves his long sword in the boat, keeps the short sword at his waist and carries only the oar sword into the duel.

A group of Kojirō supporters has violated Tadatoshi's order and waits near Hikojima with lances, ready to avenge him if he loses; officials remove them from Funashima but do not fully neutralize the risk.
Sado tells Iori to watch the duel as a life lesson, not merely as a display of technique, because Musashi is putting his life on the line before his pupil.
When Kojirō throws away his scabbard, Musashi says he has already lost because he has cast away his future and life, visibly shaking Kojirō.
After multiple exchanges, Kojirō's Drying Pole cuts away Musashi's headband, but Musashi's oar sword strikes and breaks Kojirō's skull.
Kojirō never returns to the living world. Musashi detects a faint trace of breath immediately after the blow and hopes treatment might save him, but the narrator confirms his death.
Musashi feels admiration and gratitude toward Kojirō, judging him the strongest opponent he has faced and recognizing that Kojirō forced him beyond his ordinary limits.
The narration distinguishes Kojirō's confidence in the sword of strength and skill from Musashi's trust in the sword of the spirit.
Musashi bows to Kojirō and the officials, returns to Sasuke's boat and leaves Funashima without administering a coup de grace.
The narration explicitly refuses to certify whether Kojirō's supporters attempted revenge afterward and notes that later criticism of Musashi's conduct persisted.
